newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Coffee demand may be 120 mln bags by 2005 - ICO head.
newsitem.headline: Coffee demand may be 120 mln bags by 2005 - ICO head.

text.p: World coffee consumption could reach 120 million 60-kg bags by the year 2005, the executive director of the International Coffee Organisation (ICO) said in a paper presented at a coffee seminar on Tuesday.
Celsius Lodder said in a speech delivered by the ICO's Robert Hagen in Rio, that substantial growth in emerging markets, mainly in Eastern Europe and the Far East, is likely.

Coffee consumption in established markets, which dipped when retail prices showed sharp increases in 1994, will recover and show a resumption of growth, although this is not likely to be uniform, Lodder said. He added that this also applies to the consumption trend in net coffee exporting countries.

Lodder said he looked at consumption starting from the basis of patterns over the last thirty years, commencing with the situation in 1965 and offering an indication of likely movements up to the year 2005.

The basic consumption indicators used are disappearance in the case of ICO member countries, which is derived by taking net imports and adjusting the figures for changes in large-scale inventories, and simply net imports in the case of non-member countries.
On this basis the first ten years of the period analysed, from 1965 to 1975, showed an increase from 63 to 77 million bags a year, a growth rate of 22 percent.
Growth rates in the next two decades slowed down to 13 and 10 percent respectively, with global consumption increasing from 85 million bags in 1985 to 96 million in 1995.

Because of trends in the emerging markets, the growth rate in the period from 1995 to 2005 may revert to the rates achieved in the earlier period, securing a 2.5 percent average yearly growth rate from 1995 to 2000, with achievable trend target levels of 108 million bags in 2000 and up to 120 million bags by 2005, Lodder argued.

He said it is significant that when substantial retail price increases occurred, affecting 1995 consumption, the drop of 1.5 million bags in established markets was counteracted by continued progress in the emerging areas, resulting in a total percentage drop of only 800,000 bags.

Lodder said this point could also be illustrated by an analysis of the composition of coffee consumption by broad categories. Whereas in 1965 ICO importing members accounted for 68 percent of global consumption (essentially the established markets) and non- members only 8 percent, by 1995 the latter
category had doubled to 16 percent with established markets accounting for 61 percent.
The percentage of consumption in net exporting countries remained constant at around 23 to 24 percent.

Apart from the basic ICO data Lodder said he had also taken into account the work undertaken by the organisation jointly with Market Tracking International which resulted in the Coffee International File 1995-2000, "probably the most complete recent study of the world coffee market."
He emphasised that his projections for future years are trend forecasts.
